text:
nina: Hey — planning a CI job that needs to call the redwood CLI to create embeddings and run a quick rerank. We want ephemeral profiles (one per pipeline run) rather than a single long-lived token. Looking for patterns: how have folks safely injected per-run credentials into the CLI config, and any gotchas with keyrings vs file-based tokens in containers?

sam: We do something similar. TL;DR: avoid OS keyrings in ephemeral containers. mount token as a file (tmpfs) and point the CLI at it. keep perms tight. :lock:

kevin: Example pattern that worked for us (AWS Secrets Manager -> GitHub Actions runner):

1) runner fetches secret json, writes /run/secrets/redwood_token
2) set REDWOOD_TOKEN_FILE=/run/secrets/redwood_token
3) call: `redwood config activate --profile ci-$GITHUB_RUN_ID --token-file "$REDWOOD_TOKEN_FILE"`

We left the token on tmpfs and did `shred` at the end. Also `chmod 600` before any CLI calls.

maria: If you can't use a token-file flag, you can still write directly to the config file atomically: write to a tmp file then mv. Example: 

```bash
TMP=$(mktemp)
cat > "$TMP" <<EOF
[profiles]
ci-$GITHUB_RUN_ID=token: $TOKEN
EOF
chmod 600 "$TMP"
mv "$TMP" ~/.config/redwood/credentials
# run your commands
rm ~/.config/redwood/credentials
```

jen: Note: avoid the desktop keyring/keychain in container images. The redwood CLI can fallback to env var `REDWOOD_TOKEN` too, so in many CI systems it's simplest to inject `REDWOOD_TOKEN` into the job (secrets masked), then call `redwood --profile ci-$ID embed ...` and it will use the env var. Downside: token appears in process env of cli; but that's standard.

nina: Helpful — thanks. A couple follow-ups: 1) Do we have a CLI command that rotates/profile-activates atomically? 2) Any streaming quirks when using the CLI non-interactively (e.g., `redwood chat --stream` inside a script)?

sam: 1) There isn't a single RPC that does 'write token and atomically swap profile' in older CLI builds, but `redwood config activate` (above) is atomic on most filesystems if implemented with mv. 2) For streaming: if you run `--stream` in a non-tty CI job, the CLI may use chunked outputs and flush behavior can be weird. Use `--no-stream` in batch runs, or pipe through `stdbuf -oL` if you need live tailing.

kevin: Another tip: when running multiple concurrent runners on same host, don't write to `~/.config/redwood` directly. Use `REDWOOD_CONFIG_DIR=$(mktemp -d)` per-run and export `REDWOOD_CONFIG_DIR` so each job is isolated.

maria: Also, if your CI needs to refresh tokens automatically, consider short-lived service tokens + a tiny sidecar that calls `redwood auth refresh --profile ci-$ID --refresh-token $REFRESH` and writes the new token to the file. Keep retries exponential and backoff jitter.

jen: Quick sample that uses env var fallback and isolated config dir: 

```bash
export REDWOOD_CONFIG_DIR="$(mktemp -d)"
export REDWOOD_TOKEN="$TOKEN"
# create a small wrapper for safety
redwood --profile ci-$GITHUB_RUN_ID embed create --input "$INPUT" --output out.json
# cleanup
rm -rf "$REDWOOD_CONFIG_DIR"
```

devex-bot: Reminder: check internal guidance doc `docs/ci/ephemeral-auth.md` for our recommended patterns (updated 2025-11-12).

nina: Perfect — we'll prototype with REDWOOD_CONFIG_DIR + token env fallback and short-lived tokens. I'll post results. :thumbsup:

sam: Ping me if you want a review of the script.

kevin: And add a step that validates the token works before starting expensive work, e.g. `redwood auth whoami --profile ci-$ID` to fail-fast.

maria: FYI we also encountered a streaming memory leak once when using `--stream` and large outputs; we now request smaller batch sizes and use `--no-stream` for batch pipelines.

nina: Noted. thanks everyone!
